passage:
Dear diary, Wednesday
Best lunch break ever. I told everyone about the new laptop Abbu is getting me, and the holiday abroad in May, five-star hotel, pool on the roof. Everyone went quiet, which means they were impressed. I also mentioned that the tuition teacher says I'm the smartest in the batch.
Keerthana rolled her eyes at the hotel part. Probably jealous. Then she sat with the 9B girls for the rest of lunch and didn't save me a seat on the bus. Weird. Maybe her stomach was upset.
Tomorrow I'll tell them about the concert tickets. That should get them talking again.
Honestly, though, nobody asked me anything today. They just said "nice" and looked at their phones.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Sabina say about the hotel?
qa.a: Sabina said it was five-star, with a pool on the roof.

qa.q: What does Sabina think the quiet at lunch means, and what might it really show?
qa.a: Sabina thinks it means everyone was impressed, but it may show boredom or unease, since nobody asked anything and they looked at their phones.

qa.q: What could Sabina try at tomorrow's lunch instead of talking about the concert tickets?
qa.a: Sabina could ask the others about their own week and really listen, which might bring Keerthana back more than another boast.

qa.q: How might Keerthana be feeling about Sabina's stories?
qa.a: Keerthana seems tired of the bragging; her rolled eyes and choosing the 9B table suggest she is quietly pulling away.

grounding: A teenager boasts about money and status to rank higher with the group, and misses the rolled eyes and quiet distancing around Sabina.

Naveen, you asked why I didn't post about the fellowship. Honestly, I thought about it. In first year I posted everything, every certificate, and then kept checking who had liked it. It never felt like enough.
This time I told Ammi and my lab partner, and that was it. On Monday a girl from my batch stopped me in the canteen. "Salma, heard you got the big one?" I said, "Yes, I'm really happy about it," and then asked about her placement interview, because she had been nervous all week.

I've roomed with Rehana for two years, and I found out about her university medal the way everyone else did: from the notice on the hostel board. She hadn't mentioned it.
At dinner people crowded round. "Why didn't you tell us?" someone asked. Rehana shrugged, smiling. "I only found out yesterday. I'm really pleased. It was a lot of late nights." Then she turned to me. "Devika, did your professor like the draft?"
Across the table another girl was listing her marks from every semester, louder and louder. Rehana listened, nodded and said, "That's great." She didn't compete.
I can't know what goes on in her head. But she didn't seem to need us to clap. She seemed to already know what she had done.

qa.a: Devika found out from the notice on the hostel board.

qa.a: It suggests she feels quietly proud and secure, pleased with her hard work without needing others' applause.

qa.q: Which choice in Rehana's reply stands out, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She shared the news simply and then asked about Devika's draft, which kept dinner warm instead of turning it into a contest.

qa.q: How might the girl listing her marks feel when Rehana doesn't compete?
qa.a: She might feel less need to keep proving herself, or she might notice the contrast and feel a little unsure.

You know Bhavna from my team? Everyone calls her arrogant. In every meeting she finds a way to mention the award, the client who asked for her by name, the report the director loved. People roll their eyes.
I used to as well. Then one day I saw her before a review, rereading her own old appreciation emails in the pantry, lips moving. That didn't look like arrogance. It looked like someone checking she was still good enough.

qa.a: Himani gave specific, honest praise about once a week, and Bhavna mentioned the award far less and even asked Himani for help.

Our theatre group rehearses every Sunday in the community hall, and Abhinav has a habit. Whenever the director gives him a note, within five minutes he mentions the three college plays he led, or the newspaper line that once called him "promising". The others exchange looks.
Last week I watched more closely. The listing always came right after a correction, never after praise. His voice went fast and bright, and his eyes kept checking our faces. I can't be sure, but it looked less like pride and more like someone patching a hole.
So after the run-through I told him, "That pause before your last line gave me goosebumps." He blinked. "Really? Thanks, Parveen." For the rest of the evening, he didn't mention college once.

qa.q: When did Abhinav usually mention his college plays?
qa.a: Within five minutes of the director giving him a note, right after a correction.

qa.q: What does Parveen think lies beneath Abhinav's listing, and why?
qa.a: Parveen thinks it is insecurity, like patching a hole, because it always followed a correction and his eyes kept checking faces.

qa.q: What did Parveen try, and what happened?
qa.a: Parveen gave a specific compliment about his pause before the last line, and Abhinav didn't mention college for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What might it be like for Abhinav to receive the director's notes?
qa.a: Corrections may sting and make him worry he isn't good enough, so he reaches for old successes to feel steady.

grounding: A member of a theatre group notices a peer's boasting follows every correction, reads it as insecurity, and eases it with specific praise.

At the bus stand in their small town, Vidya told anyone who would listen that Jasleen had simply changed. "She found new friends in the other section and dropped me. Totally fake." Her cousin nodded along on the ride home.
Vidya left out Jasleen's birthday, when she had laughed with the others at Jasleen's homemade cake, and the message Jasleen sent afterwards, which Vidya never answered. Whenever that memory came up, she pushed it away and went back to the easier version.
A month later, at the temple fair, Vidya snapped at a new girl from her class for being late and walked off. Standing alone by the bangle stalls, she felt a flicker of the same heavy feeling. She didn't let herself look at it.

qa.q: What did Vidya say Jasleen had done?
qa.a: Vidya said Jasleen found new friends in the other section and dropped her.

qa.q: Why does Vidya keep going back to the easier version?
qa.a: It eases her guilt about laughing at Jasleen's homemade cake and ignoring her message, so she avoids the memory.

qa.q: What could Vidya do when that heavy feeling comes back?
qa.a: She could let herself look at the birthday memory honestly, perhaps talk it through with someone she trusts, and think about answering Jasleen.

qa.q: How might Jasleen tell the story of the lost friendship?
qa.a: Jasleen would probably remember being laughed at on her birthday and an unanswered message, not simply changing and dropping Vidya.

grounding: A teenage girl blames a lost friend entirely, and the flattering story eases her guilt while blocking the learning she needs for the next friendship.

In Oslo the snow had turned grey, and Astrid stamped it off her boots in the hallway. "Mei sat with the new girl again," she told her mother. "She's so two-faced. I did nothing."
Her mother looked up from the soup. "Nothing at all? Didn't you two argue after the concert?"
"That was ages ago. And she was being dramatic."
Astrid didn't mention that she had told the choir girls Mei's secret about her parents' divorce, the one Mei had begged her to keep. She had almost forgotten it herself, or rather had stopped letting herself remember.
"Maybe ask her what happened from her side?" her mother said.
"Why should I? She's the problem." Astrid went to her room and shut the door, and the version where she did nothing felt safe again.

qa.a: Astrid told them Mei's secret about her parents' divorce, the one Mei had begged her to keep.

qa.q: Why does Astrid insist she did nothing?
qa.a: Remembering that she spilled Mei's secret would bring guilt, so the story where Mei is the problem feels safer.

qa.q: What would help Astrid learn from this before her next friendship?
qa.a: She could take her mother's suggestion, ask Mei about her side, and own up to sharing the secret, which could begin a repair.

qa.q: What is it like for Mei after her secret was shared?
qa.a: Mei probably feels betrayed and exposed, so keeping away from Astrid may be her way of protecting herself.

grounding: A teenage girl insists Mei is the only problem, and the flattering story keeps her from facing the guilt that could teach her something.

Three weeks before the semester exams, Wasim's desk in the paying-guest room was covered in charger cables and unopened notes. "Relax," he told his classmate Disha on a call. "I work better under pressure. Last-minute is my style."
He said it every evening, between long cricket videos and trips to the chai stall. It sounded confident. Inside, it was different. Every time he opened the thermodynamics book, he remembered the forty-one he had got in the mid-term, and his chest tightened. Closing the book felt like relief.
On the Sunday before exams he finally opened it at midnight and couldn't follow the first chapter. "Pressure" felt a lot like panic. He messaged Disha: "Can we study together tomorrow? Honestly, I think I've been scared of this subject."

qa.a: Wasim got forty-one in the mid-term.

qa.a: He was afraid of failing again; remembering the forty-one tightened his chest, and closing the book brought relief.

qa.a: Disha might have believed it at first, but the honest message shows the confidence was covering fear.

grounding: A student skips weeks of study and calls it working better under pressure, a story that shields him from his fear of failing.

"I'm resting my brain, Didi. I study best in the last two weeks. Always have."

In Cape Town, Daniel's kitchen drawer was full of envelopes he hadn't opened. Most had the bank's red stripe on the front. When a new one came, he slid it under the others without looking.
"It'll sort itself out," he told Lindiwe, his flatmate, when she noticed the drawer wouldn't close. "Bonus season's coming. I'll handle it then." He said it lightly, but he switched to talking about football so fast that she stopped mid-sentence.
Last year's bonus had been smaller than promised. He knew that. He also knew that opening the envelopes would mean numbers, and numbers would mean doing something he didn't feel ready to do.
"There's a free advice centre near my work," Lindiwe said. "I could come with you." Daniel nodded at the kettle. "After payday, maybe."

qa.q: What was on the front of most of the envelopes?
qa.a: Most had the bank's red stripe on the front.

qa.q: Why does Daniel avoid opening the envelopes?
qa.a: Opening them would mean facing the numbers and having to act, which he doesn't feel ready for, so avoiding them feels safer.

qa.q: What protective step does Lindiwe offer, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She offers to go with him to a free advice centre, because qualified help and a supportive flatmate can make facing the problem less frightening.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Daniel changes the subject so fast?
qa.a: She may feel shut out and worried, since she noticed the drawer and was cut off mid-sentence.

grounding: A young man with mounting bills keeps saying it will sort itself out, because looking straight at the numbers would demand action he is not ready for.

Dear Kalyani,
Remember how I kept calling my job "just a rough patch"? Last night I tried the trick you taught me. I pretended you had told me the same story: your boss takes credit for your work, you haven't learned anything new in a year, and you cry on Sunday nights. I knew straight away what I'd say to you: "That isn't a rough patch. That's a pattern."
Then I asked myself the second question: what would change my mind? If my boss credited me even once in the next month, maybe. I wrote that on a sticky note and put it on the fridge.
I didn't shout at myself or call myself stupid. I just looked at it. It was oddly calm.
With love,
Baljeet

qa.a: Baljeet put the sticky note on the fridge.

qa.a: It lets Baljeet see the situation with the kindness and clarity used for someone else, so the "rough patch" turns out to be a pattern.

qa.a: Baljeet decided that would be real evidence, so the "rough patch" story might then be worth another look.

Mehak, you asked how I finally decided about the bakery. For three years I said, "Next season it'll pick up." Every season I said it. Then one night, instead of arguing with myself, I asked a kinder question: "Farhan, if your best friend told you this, what would you say?" I knew the answer. I'd say, "Show me the numbers, yaar."
So I asked the second question: what would actually change my mind? I wrote it down. If orders don't grow by Diwali, I stop and look for a job. No drama, no calling myself a failure.
Diwali came. They didn't grow. It hurt, but it didn't feel like defeat. It felt like I had finally been honest with someone I care about. Me.

qa.q: What test did Farhan write down?
qa.a: If orders don't grow by Diwali, Farhan stops and looks for a job.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when orders didn't grow by Diwali?
qa.a: It hurt, but Farhan didn't feel defeated; it felt like finally being honest with someone Farhan cares about.

qa.q: Which question was the turning point for Farhan, and why?
qa.a: Asking what to say if a best friend told the same story, because it replaced self-argument with a kind, clear view.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel hearing how Farhan decided?
qa.a: Mehak might feel relieved that the decision came from calm honesty rather than harsh self-blame.

grounding: A young adult tests a hopeful story about a struggling bakery with kind questions and a clear piece of evidence, instead of harsh self-attack.

In Nairobi, Wanjiru hugged her little brother Sami after he cried over her new crayons. "I promise I'll share them forever and ever," she said, and she meant it with her whole body.
The next morning Sami reached for the purple one. Wanjiru snatched the box. "Mine!"
"You promised," Sami wailed.
Wanjiru looked confused, then cross, then sad. Yesterday's promise felt very far away. Mama knelt down. "Promises are for tomorrow-you too," she said softly. "Shall we choose which colours Sami can use today?"

Suraj (8) spent the afternoon helping Gautam finish a surprise card for Gautam's mother's birthday. Gautam made him promise not to tell.
